column1: What is YouTube's fundamental architectural function as a platform, beyond hosting video?
column2: It is a two-sided market solving the discovery problem—connecting creators' content to the exact viewers who want it—through algorithmic curation and monetization infrastructure.

column1: What is the first critical invariant of YouTube's platform architecture?
column2: Engagement maximization bias is encoded into every layer (recommendation engine, comments, notifications, analytics)—the platform optimizes for watch time, not truth or artistic merit.

column1: What is the power asymmetry invariant in YouTube's platform design?
column2: YouTube owns the platform, algorithm, distribution, and monetization rules; creators own content but not the audience relationship; viewers own attention but often lack awareness of why they're shown what they see.

column1: Why did YouTube shift from view-count optimization to watch-time optimization around 2012?
column2: View counts rewarded clickbait and sensationalism disconnected from content quality; watch time better correlated with ad inventory exposure and user satisfaction—though it introduced new distortions like artificially padded video lengths.

column1: What unintended consequence emerged from YouTube's watch-time optimization metric?
column2: Creators padded videos to cross algorithmic length thresholds and exploited endless live-streams for passive background watch-time accumulation, regardless of actual viewer engagement quality.

column1: What is the 'attention arbitrage' principle underlying YouTube monetization?
column2: Google acquires human attention via YouTube, packages it into measurable/targetable ad impressions, and sells access to advertisers; creators function as attention aggregators that Google monetizes on their behalf.

column1: What is CPM and why is it called the 'universal exchange rate' for creators?
column2: CPM (Cost Per Mille) is the dollar amount advertisers pay per thousand impressions; it's the gravitational center of creator economics, explaining why niches like finance/tech attract creators despite similar view counts to lower-CPM niches.

column1: Name the three invariant constraints shaping creator behavior in the monetization system.
column2: 1) Asymmetric information (opaque algorithm/analytics), 2) Algorithmic dependency (income tied to algorithmic promotion), 3) Policy fragility (unilateral, opaque demonetization with minimal recourse).

column1: What core invariant drives YouTube's content moderation challenges?
column2: Asymmetric information under time pressure: millions of hours upload daily, making human moderation at scale impossible, forcing automated systems to make fast binary decisions with incomplete context, producing systematic false positives/negatives.

column1: What two competing pressures shaped YouTube's content moderation architecture?
column2: Section 230 Safe Harbor (incentivizes reactive moderation to avoid publisher liability) vs. advertiser pressure post-2017 Adpocalypse (incentivizes aggressive proactive enforcement for brand safety).

column1: Describe YouTube's 'layered governance stack' for content moderation.
column2: Policy definition (Community Guidelines) → automated signal detection (ML classifiers, Content ID) → human review (global contractor moderators) → strike-based account degradation → limited appeals mechanism.

column1: Mechanically, why does radicalization occur via YouTube's recommendation algorithm without centralized coordination?
column2: The algorithm optimizes purely for predicted watch time; since extremity correlates with higher engagement, it progressively surfaces more extreme content sharing similar engagement patterns—a mechanical consequence, not deliberate design.
